title: Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL)
summary: Defines the Simple Authentication and Security Layer, a framework for authentication and data security in connection-oriented protocols through replaceable mechanisms. It lets new protocols reuse existing mechanisms and old protocols adopt new ones. It obsoletes RFC 2222 and is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: SASL is a framework that lets connection-based protocols reuse authentication methods. A mechanism can also negotiate a security layer to protect later data, if both the mechanism and protocol support it.

questions: what is the sasl external mechanism
what is a sasl security layer
subtitle: A reusable framework for authentication and optional data protection in connection-based protocols.

tldr.problem: Each connection-oriented protocol should not need to invent its own authentication methods or data-protection layer.
tldr.mechanism: SASL separates protocol-specific message exchange from replaceable authentication mechanisms and can install a security layer after success.
tldr.outcome: Protocols can reuse mechanisms, and mechanisms can work with multiple protocols. The framework itself does not guarantee protection against downgrade or other attacks.

today: RFC 4422 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 2222. It defines the SASL framework and the EXTERNAL mechanism; other mechanisms have separate specifications.

sections.title: A Shared Layer for Protocols and Mechanisms
sections.content:
The Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) provides a structured interface between connection-oriented protocols and replaceable authentication mechanisms. A new protocol can reuse an existing mechanism, and an existing protocol can use a newer mechanism.

SASL can also provide a security layer for later protocol exchanges. The mechanism defines its security services; the protocol defines how to carry the exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: SASL separates the conversation a protocol uses from the authentication method it uses. That lets the two parts change independently.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization Identities
sections.content:
SASL distinguishes the authentication identity associated with a client's credentials from the authorization identity the client asks to act as. If the authorization identity is absent or empty, the client asks to act as the identity associated with its credentials.

The server verifies the credentials and whether that identity may act as the requested authorization identity. The exact forms of these identities are defined by the mechanism and the application protocol, not by the SASL framework.
sections.plainLanguage: One identity proves which credentials the client has; another names the account or role it wants to use. The server checks both the credentials and permission to act as that identity.

sections.title: The Challenge-and-Response Exchange
sections.content:
The client starts an exchange by naming a mechanism. The server and client then send one or more challenge-response pairs, after which the server reports success or failure. Some mechanisms let the client send an initial response with its first message.

Mechanism negotiation is specific to the protocol and is not protected by the later authentication exchange. An attacker may change the available-mechanism list unless another protection or post-authentication check detects that change.
sections.plainLanguage: The client chooses a mechanism, answers the server's challenges, and receives an outcome. The protocol must protect or recheck the mechanism choice if downgrade attacks matter.

sections.title: Installing a Security Layer
sections.content:
If authentication succeeds and the parties negotiated a security layer, the server installs it after reporting the outcome and the client installs it after receiving that outcome. The layer takes effect at the point specified by the application protocol.

Protected data is sent in buffers preceded by a four-octet length. If a received buffer exceeds the size the other side agreed to accept, the receiver should close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A negotiated security layer protects protocol data after authentication finishes. The protocol must say exactly where protection starts.

sections.title: Security Limits and Downgrade Risks
sections.content:
SASL mechanisms differ in what they protect; some do not provide strong protection against passive or active attacks, and some do not provide a security layer. The framework is also vulnerable to downgrade attacks when an attacker can alter mechanism negotiation.

Implementations should enforce minimum security requirements and verify that the completed exchange meets them. RFC 4422 obsoletes RFC 2222; several mechanisms are specified separately or treated as obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: SASL does not make every mechanism equally secure. Each side must reject choices that fall below its security requirements.
